sentences.text: Its skull differed from other members of the family by being short and solid, resembling a miniature Tyrannosaurus.
It is very likely that this animal was covered in feathers, as has been proven in other dromaeosaurids like Velociraptor or Microraptor.
The sickle claw on its foot was of intermediate size compared to other dromaeosaurids and would have been used to grip prey and inflict serious wounds.
Despite popular casts in museums worldwide, Dromaeosaurus is actually poorly known from real fossil evidence and is known from surprisingly few actual fossils.
The generic name Dromaeosaurus derives from the Greek words dromeus meaning 'runner' and sauros meaning 'lizard'.
Researchers estimated Dromaeosaurus had a bite nearly three times stronger than Velociraptor's, suggesting it relied more on its jaws than its sickle claw for killing prey.

The type species Dromaeosaurus albertensis was described by William Diller Matthew and Barnum Brown in 1922 after the first remains were found by Barnum Brown in 1914 near the Red Deer River in Alberta.

D. albertensis is the type specimen and the most complete known member of the genus, and the family dromaeosaurids is named after it, though due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil material, only the type species is considered valid.
Matthew and Brown originally classified Dromaeosaurus in the subfamily Dromaeosaurinae within the family Deinodontidae, now known as Tyrannosauridae.
Dromaeosaurus used a characteristic 'puncture and pull' feeding method typical of coelurosaurian theropods.

Studies suggest Dromaeosaurus included bone in its diet and was better adapted to attack struggling prey compared to troodontids that ate softer animals and carrion, while the same study indicated that both Dromaeosaurus and Saurornitholestes likely included bone in their diet.
Dromaeosaurus could hunt prey similar to or larger than itself, such as ornithomimids, ornithopods, and juvenile ceratopsians, while not ignoring smaller prey like lizards and mammals.
Dromaeosaurus had notably large eyes providing good vision, along with well-developed smell and hearing.

The tail of Dromaeosaurus was rigid except at the base, with thin, flexible bone rods that likely acted as a rudder to help change direction quickly during a run and maintain flight trajectory during a jump toward prey, and its rigid tail allowed Dromaeosaurus to maintain balance while running at speeds over 40 km/h.

The discovery of the sister species Dakotaraptor, which has a larger flexor tubercle than most other dromaeosaurids, supports the suggestion that Dromaeosaurus used its sickle claw less than other dromaeosaurids.
In 1969, John H. Ostrom assigned Dromaeosaurus to the family Dromaeosauridae based on shared features with Velociraptor and Deinonychus.
Teeth attributed to Dromaeosaurus have been found in the Prince Creek Formation.
Dromaeosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, between 80 and 69 million years ago, from the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages.
Dromaeosaurus lived in what is now North America.
It is debated whether the unusual, grooved 'Dromaeosaurus morphotype A' teeth found in Alberta belong to Dromaeosaurus, as their origin remains confusing.
The exact relationships of Dromaeosaurus are unclear, and it is debated whether its robust construction makes it appear primitive despite being a highly specialized animal.
The exact evolutionary relationships of Dromaeosaurus remain somewhat unclear among scientists.
